passage: "First thing I say in every presentation now is: 'I'm Wasim, I stutter, and I'll get there.' Then I carry on. Took me three years to say that line. In first year I'd apologise every time I blocked. 'S-sorry, sorry.' I'd end up apologising more than presenting. People would jump in and finish my sentences. Kind, I guess, but it made me feel like a kid. What changed was a support group my speech therapist told me about. Fifteen people on video calls every Thursday. One of them was a lawyer! For the first time I wasn't the only one. Now I slow down on purpose. I pause. I don't say sorry. And I notice who waits. Deepak, my project partner, keeps looking right at me and just waits. Those people make it so much easier."

qa.q: What is the first thing Wasim says in every presentation now?
qa.a: I'm Wasim, I stutter, and I'll get there.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when people finished Wasim's sentences?
qa.a: Wasim felt small and embarrassed, as if treated like a kid, even though the others meant to be kind.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Wasim speak with confidence?
qa.a: Joining a support group through the speech therapist, where Wasim was no longer the only one.

qa.q: How does Deepak's way of listening affect Wasim?
qa.a: Deepak keeps looking at Wasim and waits, which makes speaking much easier.

grounding: It shows a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering, slows down without apologising, and is helped by patient listeners and a support group.

passage: I'm Manoj. I sat beside Jahnavi on her first client call last month, and I still think about it. She'd joined our team two weeks before. When the call started, she said, clear as anything, "Hi, I'm Jahnavi. I stutter, so sometimes I'll take a moment. The numbers are worth the wait." The client laughed and said, "No problem." Then she walked them through the whole budget. She blocked a couple of times on words starting with "p". She paused, didn't apologise, and carried on. The client kept waiting and nodding. After the call I asked, "Weren't you nervous?" She shrugged. "Less than I used to be. I go to a support group on Thursdays. Makes me feel less alone." The client emailed next day, asking specifically for her.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say at the start of the call?
qa.a: Hi, I'm Jahnavi. I stutter, so sometimes I'll take a moment. The numbers are worth the wait.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi's shrug and answer suggest about how she feels about speaking now?
qa.a: It suggests she still feels some nerves but is much more confident, helped by the support group.

qa.q: Which of Jahnavi's choices made the call go smoothly?
qa.a: She told the client about her stutter at the start, paused without apologising, and kept going.

qa.q: How did the client respond to Jahnavi's openness?
qa.a: The client laughed kindly, kept waiting and nodding, and later asked for her specifically.

grounding: A colleague describes a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering, pauses without apologising, and is helped by patient listeners and a support group.

passage:
First week of college: at the photography club, Joseph stood up to introduce himself. His throat locked on the J. He paused, then said, "I stutter, so give me a second. J-Joseph. I shoot street photos." Nobody laughed. Ira, in the front, kept looking at him, waiting.
Third week: Joseph presented his street series. He slowed down on purpose, stuck on "market" twice, and didn't say sorry once. Ira asked the first question.
Sixth week: Joseph went to a stuttering support group at the city library. Eight people sat in a circle, trading stories about phone calls and job interviews. For the first time, he didn't feel like the only one. He walked out laughing with a man who stuttered on every B.

qa.q: What does Joseph photograph?
qa.a: He shoots street photos.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel at the support group?
qa.a: He felt less alone and relieved, laughing with another member and no longer feeling like the only one.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that shows confident speaking?
qa.a: He named his stutter openly, slowed down on purpose and did not apologise during his presentation.

qa.q: How might Ira have seen Joseph at the club?
qa.a: Ira likely saw him as confident and interesting, keeping eye contact, waiting patiently and asking the first question about his photos.

grounding: Shows a young adult speaking openly about stuttering, slowing down without apology, helped by a patient listener and a support group.

passage: "Nilesh, sit, sit. You're worried about Monday's client pitch because of your stutter? Let me tell you something. When I was twenty-two, in my first job at the bank, I stuttered so badly I used to hide in the store room when the phone rang. My first presentation, I apologised eleven times. My manager, Mr D'Souza, stopped me after. He said, 'Yogesh, stop saying sorry. Just say it slowly. We'll wait.' And he did. He looked me in the eye every time. A colleague told me about a stuttering group that met at a temple hall on Sundays. I went, terrified. Twenty people like me! After that I started every meeting saying, 'I stutter, bear with me.' Never apologised again. So, Monday, you slow down. I'll be in the room."

qa.q: How many times did Yogesh apologise in that first presentation?
qa.a: Yogesh apologised eleven times.

qa.q: How did young Yogesh feel going to the stuttering group for the first time?
qa.a: Yogesh felt terrified at first, then surprised and relieved to find twenty people in the same boat.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Yogesh spoke?
qa.a: Mr D'Souza told Yogesh to stop apologising and slow down, then waited patiently with eye contact, and Yogesh later found a support group.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Souza have seen young Yogesh?
qa.a: He likely saw a capable young employee worth waiting for, not someone who needed to apologise.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to speak openly about stuttering, slow down without apologising, helped by a patient manager and a support group.

passage: The interview panel was running late, and the coordinator told Hemant, twenty-two, "You'll only get ten minutes, sorry." His heart sank; ten minutes felt like nothing for someone who stutters. He walked in and sat down. "Before we start, I stutter. I'll take my time, and I'll get there." The main interviewer, Ritu, nodded and kept her eyes on him. When he stuck on "project," she waited. He didn't apologise. He explained his water-sensor design clearly, slowly, point by point. At the end Ritu said, "That was the clearest explanation today." Outside, he texted his support group: "Did it. Didn't say sorry once." Three replies came back in a minute.

qa.q: How many minutes did the coordinator say Hemant would get?
qa.a: The coordinator said he would only get ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when told he would get only ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and worried, his heart sinking, since he stutters and the time felt short.

qa.q: What choices helped Hemant speak with confidence?
qa.a: He named his stutter at the start, took his time and did not apologise, explaining his design point by point.

qa.q: How did Ritu see Hemant's explanation?
qa.a: Ritu found it the clearest explanation of the day, and she showed respect by waiting and keeping eye contact.

grounding: Shows a young adult who speaks openly about stuttering and does not apologise, helped by a patient listener and a support group, despite time pressure.

passage:
The seminar room at the Chennai college was full when Vidya stood up to present. "Before I start," she said, "I stutter. Some words take longer. I'll get there."
She spoke slowly. On "p-p-population" she paused, breathed and carried on. She didn't say sorry once.
In the front row, Payal kept her eyes on Vidya's face and nodded, waiting. The professor didn't rush her either.
At the end, a student asked a sharp question about her data, and Vidya answered it fully. Afterwards Payal said, "That was brilliant."
"Two years ago I'd have skipped this," Vidya admitted. "I felt like the only person in the world who talked like me. Then I found a Saturday support group for people who stutter. Turns out, I wasn't alone."

qa.q: What does Vidya go to on Saturdays?
qa.a: A support group for people who stutter.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel two years ago?
qa.a: She felt lonely and isolated, like the only person in the world who talked like her.

qa.q: What helped Vidya present with confidence?
qa.a: Naming her stutter openly, slowing down without apologising, patient listeners who kept eye contact, and the support group that made her feel less alone.

qa.q: How does Payal see Vidya's presentation?
qa.a: She admires it and calls it brilliant, focusing on Vidya's ideas rather than the pauses.

grounding: Vidya speaks openly about her stutter, slows down without apologising, is helped by patient listeners, and a support group eased her isolation.
